items.explanation: Postwar consumers bought cars, homes, and appliances on a tidal wave of advertising — but stock speculation was not the engine; most families bought goods, not equities.
options: A. A renewed rush to buy stocks
B. Surging automobile purchases
C. A boom in home buying
D. The power of advertising
items.stem: Consumer spending rose in the 1950s because of all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the exception. There was no renewed rush to buy stocks in the 1950s — most families bought cars, homes, and appliances, not equities. Stock speculation did not drive the consumer boom.
option_explanations.B: Surging automobile purchases really did drive 1950s consumer spending — cars were the decade's defining purchase. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: A boom in home buying really did drive spending — suburban homeownership exploded with the GI Bill and Levittowns. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: The power of advertising really did drive spending — television ads created mass consumer desire. This is not the exception.

items.explanation: Like Coolidge, Eisenhower was a pro-business fiscal conservative who left the New Deal largely intact — 'dynamic conservatism' in a gray flannel suit.
options: A. Franklin Roosevelt
B. William Howard Taft
C. Calvin Coolidge
D. Theodore Roosevelt
items.stem: Eisenhower's presidency most resembled that of

option_explanations.A: Eisenhower did not resemble Franklin Roosevelt — FDR expanded government dramatically while Eisenhower was a fiscal conservative who restrained it. They were opposites in governing philosophy.
option_explanations.B: Eisenhower did not especially resemble William Howard Taft — Taft was a Progressive-era trustbuster, while Eisenhower's 'dynamic conservatism' accepted the New Deal and focused on balanced budgets and business confidence.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Like Coolidge, Eisenhower was a pro-business fiscal conservative who left the New Deal largely intact — restraint on spending, friendliness to business, and acceptance of the existing welfare state.
option_explanations.D: Eisenhower did not resemble Theodore Roosevelt — TR was an activist trust-busting progressive, while Eisenhower governed as a restrained, business-friendly conservative.

items.explanation: Scarred by depression and war, the new suburban generation turned inward to family and showered their children with the things they had lacked — while remaining deeply suspicious of buying on credit.
options: A. They turned inward to family
B. They gave their children what they had lacked
C. They bought freely on credit
D. Both A and B
items.stem: How did Depression and war shape the generation raising families in the 1950s?

option_explanations.A: True: scarred by depression and war, the new suburban generation really did turn inward to family life. This is true but only half the answer — the question asks for the full picture.
option_explanations.B: True: they really did shower their children with the things they themselves had lacked. This is true but only half the answer.
option_explanations.C: The opposite of the generation's attitude — they remained deeply suspicious of buying on credit, remembering the debt disasters of the Depression. Free spending on credit was not their way.
option_explanations.D: Correct — both A and B. Depression and war made the new suburban generation turn inward to family AND give their children what they had lacked — while remaining deeply suspicious of buying on credit.

items.explanation: Early television's deepest effect was cultural uniformity — the same shows, ads, and values beamed into millions of living rooms, pressing Americans toward conformity.
options: A. It supplied escapist comedy
B. It delivered the day's news
C. It imposed social conformity
D. It nurtured a youth culture
items.stem: Television's most important early-1950s impact was that

option_explanations.A: Television did supply escapist comedy, but comedy was not its most important impact — its deepest effect was beaming the same shows, ads, and values into millions of living rooms, pressing Americans toward conformity.
option_explanations.B: Television did deliver the news, but news was not its most important early-1950s impact — the medium's power was cultural: standardizing tastes, values, and lifestyles across the country.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Early television's most important impact was imposing social conformity — the same programs, advertisements, and ideals entering millions of homes created a powerful pressure toward sameness.
option_explanations.D: Television did not nurture a youth culture in the early 1950s — early TV was family programming aimed at the suburban household. A distinct youth culture came later, with rock 'n' roll and the 1960s.

items.explanation: Elvis was Southern and working-class, but what truly alarmed respectable America was that rock 'n' roll's roots — and many of its musicians — were Black.
options: A. Many of its musicians and roots were Black
B. Its stars came from lower-class backgrounds
C. Its stars came from the South
D. Its lyrics promoted communism
items.stem: Many Americans especially feared rock 'n' roll because

option_explanations.A: Correct. What truly alarmed respectable America was that rock 'n' roll's roots — and many of its musicians — were Black: the music grew out of rhythm and blues, and its crossing of the color line frightened a segregated society.
option_explanations.B: Elvis was working-class, but class was not what especially frightened Americans — working-class stars were common. The racial dimension was the deeper alarm.
option_explanations.C: Elvis was Southern, but Southern origins alone did not cause the fear — country music was Southern too. What frightened people was the music's Black roots.
option_explanations.D: Rock lyrics did not promote communism — the songs were about love, cars, and dancing. Communism was never the issue; race and sexuality were.

items.explanation: The passage's whole message is trust instinct over expertise: 'what good mothers and fathers instinctively feel like doing for their babies is usually best after all' -- 'Better to make a few mistakes from being natural than to try to do everything letter-perfect out of a feeling of worry.' Spock was rebuking the rigid, schedule-driven experts of the 1920s-30s, not endorsing strictness, boarding schools, or coldness.
options: A. Trust their natural instincts rather than rigid schedules
B. Follow strict feeding and sleeping schedules
C. Send young children to boarding schools
D. Avoid physical affection with their babies
items.stem: Spock's advice differed from earlier child-rearing experts in urging parents to
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

Dr. Benjamin Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946) reassured parents that child-rearing was a natural process: trust your instincts, the book counseled, for 'you know more than you think you do' — a permissive message that resonated with a generation raising children in unprecedented prosperity.
—After Dr. Benjamin Spock, Baby and Child Care, 1946

option_explanations.A: Correct. Spock's message was trust your natural instincts: 'what good mothers and fathers instinctively feel like doing for their babies is usually best after all.' He was rebuking the rigid, schedule-driven experts of the 1920s–30s, not endorsing strictness.
option_explanations.B: The opposite of Spock's advice — strict feeding and sleeping schedules were the old expert orthodoxy he was attacking. He told parents to relax, not to regiment.
option_explanations.C: Spock never advised sending young children to boarding schools. His book was about parents raising children at home with confidence, not about institutionalizing them.
option_explanations.D: The opposite of Spock's advice — he encouraged affection and natural warmth, not coldness. Avoiding physical affection was the old rigid school's style, which he rejected.

items.explanation: Spock's Baby and Child Care was the flagship of a new postwar expert culture -- pediatricians, child psychologists, and advice columnists guiding suburban family life. Medical authority did not decline; it expanded into the nursery. The government ran no nurseries, and Victorian manuals were exactly what Spock displaced.
options: A. The decline of medical and scientific authority
B. A government takeover of child-rearing
C. A new expert culture of child psychology shaping family life
D. A return to Victorian child-rearing manuals
items.stem: Spock's reassuring guidance to parents reflected which broader postwar trend?
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

Dr. Benjamin Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946) reassured parents that child-rearing was a natural process: trust your instincts, the book counseled, for 'you know more than you think you do' — a permissive message that resonated with a generation raising children in unprecedented prosperity.
—After Dr. Benjamin Spock, Baby and Child Care, 1946

option_explanations.A: Medical and scientific authority did not decline — it expanded. Spock's book was itself an exercise of expert authority over family life, not a retreat from it.
option_explanations.B: There was no government takeover of child-rearing — no state nurseries or federal parenting programs. Spock's influence came through books and media, not government.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Spock's Baby and Child Care was the flagship of a new postwar expert culture — pediatricians, child psychologists, and advice columnists guiding suburban family life. His authority over the nursery was expert authority, newly extended.
option_explanations.D: Victorian child-rearing manuals were exactly what Spock displaced — rigid, moralistic, and strict. His permissive guidance was the break from them, not a return.

items.explanation: Like Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946), Julia Child's Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961) and her television show made an expert into a trusted household guide for suburban domestic life -- instruction as mass entertainment. Hoover, McCarthy, and Salk wielded entirely different kinds of authority.
options: A. J. Edgar Hoover's leadership of the FBI
B. Julia Child, who similarly used mass media to instruct suburban homemakers
C. Joseph McCarthy's anti-communist crusade
D. Jonas Salk's development of the polio vaccine
items.stem: Spock's role as a trusted expert guiding postwar domestic life is most comparable to that of
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

Dr. Benjamin Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946) reassured parents that child-rearing was a natural process: trust your instincts, the book counseled, for 'you know more than you think you do' — a permissive message that resonated with a generation raising children in unprecedented prosperity.
—After Dr. Benjamin Spock, Baby and Child Care, 1946

option_explanations.A: J. Edgar Hoover wielded a different kind of authority — law enforcement and surveillance, not trusted domestic guidance. His FBI leadership has nothing in common with Spock's role in the home.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Like Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946), Julia Child's cookbook (1961) and television show made an expert into a trusted household guide for suburban domestic life — instruction as mass entertainment.
option_explanations.C: Joseph McCarthy's anti-communist crusade was political persecution, not trusted household guidance. His authority was fear, not the friendly expertise Spock and Child offered.
option_explanations.D: Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was a medical breakthrough, not ongoing household instruction. Salk saved lives with a vaccine; Spock and Child guided daily domestic life through mass media.
